title: Scratch control blocks - forever, if-then, wait, broadcast
subject: cs
definition:
Control blocks in Scratch are the yellow-orange blocks that do not draw costumes, move the sprite, or play music by themselves, but they decide when, how often, and under what conditions the other blocks run. In Class 6 you focus on four of them: the forever block, the if-then block, the wait block, and the broadcast block. They belong to the Control category, and together they turn a simple list of instructions into a real program that can repeat, decide, pause, and talk between sprites.

The forever block is a C-shaped loop. When the script reaches it, it runs every block inside from top to bottom, then jumps back to the first block and runs them all again, without stopping. It is used to keep an animation or game running continuously. For example, in a project about a Bengal tiger walking in the Sundarbans, you can place a `next costume` block and a `move 10 steps` block inside a `forever`, and the tiger will keep prowling across the stage until the user clicks the red stop sign or a stop block is used.

The if-then block is the decision maker. Its top has a hexagonal gap where a condition block fits, such as `touching mouse-pointer?` or `key space pressed?`. If the condition is true when the block is reached, the blocks inside it run once; if the condition is false, the whole body is skipped and the script continues below. In an Indian classroom scene, you might make a chalk-board sprite say "Hello, students!" only if the teacher sprite is touching it.

The wait block is a timed pause. When the script reaches `wait 2 secs`, that script stops for exactly two seconds before the next block below runs. Other scripts and other sprites are not affected; the wait belongs only to the script it lives in. This is useful for pacing an animation, such as holding a green light for five seconds in a traffic-light project outside a Mumbai school.

The broadcast block sends a named message to all sprites and the stage. Any sprite that has a matching `when I receive` event hat will start its own script. This lets one sprite trigger another. In a Republic Day parade in Delhi, one sprite can `broadcast next tableau` and several other sprites can begin moving at the same time. A forever-if combination is not a separate block, but the everyday practice of placing an if-then block inside a forever loop so the condition is checked again and again, like a watchman at a railway gate.

These four blocks answer the four big questions of program flow: how to repeat, how to choose, how to delay, and how to communicate between sprites.
eli5: Imagine your Scratch stage is a playground. Control blocks are the rules of the games. The forever block makes the same game repeat again and again. The if-then block is a rule that says "do this only if something is true." The wait block is a short nap before the next move. The broadcast block is a whistle that every player can hear, and each player can decide what to do when the whistle blows.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What is the difference between the forever block and the if-then block? Give one practical example for each.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The forever block and the if-then block are both control blocks, but they solve different problems. The forever block is a loop that runs the blocks inside it again and again without stopping. Once the script enters the forever, it follows the stacked blocks from top to bottom, jumps back to the start, and repeats. It is the right choice when you want continuous animation or action, such as making a kite sprite in a Makar Sankranti scene keep flying across the sky. The if-then block, on the other hand, is a conditional or decision block. It looks at a condition in its hexagonal slot, which can be true or false. If the condition is true, the blocks inside the if-then run once; if the condition is false, they are skipped. It is the right choice when you want a one-time decision, such as making the kite say "I am stuck!" only if it touches a tree. In short, forever is about repetition, while if-then is about selection. A clever Class 6 project combines them by placing an if-then inside a forever, so the condition is checked repeatedly while the animation keeps running.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A classmate says, "The wait block stops the whole Scratch program for the given time." Do you agree? Justify your answer.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I do not agree with the statement because the wait block does not stop the whole Scratch program. It is a local pause, which means it stops only the script in which it is placed for the number of seconds written in the block. While that one script waits, other scripts on the same sprite and scripts on other sprites continue to run normally. For example, if a sprite in a Republic Day parade says "Jai Hind!" and then waits 2 seconds, only the script that contains the wait is delayed. Another sprite can still be marching because it has its own script. If the wait were a global pause, every animation on the stage would freeze at once, which would not be useful. The wait block is therefore best used to create a short delay or a rhythm, such as holding a traffic-light colour before it changes. It is different from the stop all block, which really does end every script. A good way to remember this is: wait pauses one script, not the whole stage.

diagnosticQuestions.question: "The broadcast block and the say block do the same job, because both can make another sprite do something." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is mostly wrong, but it contains one small grain of truth that needs careful examination. The broadcast block sends a message, such as `goal` or `start dance`, to all sprites and the stage. Any sprite that has a matching `when I receive` hat will run the script attached to it. The say block, however, displays a speech bubble above the sprite that runs it; it does not send a message to other sprites or start their scripts. Therefore the two blocks do very different jobs. The small grain of truth is that a broadcast can lead to another sprite doing something, but only if that sprite already has the right receive hat. Even then, the broadcast is not a command to a specific sprite; it is an announcement to everyone, and each listener chooses whether to act. The say block is only about showing text on the screen and is found in the Looks category, not the Control category. A correct explanation would be that broadcast is the Control block for inter-sprite messaging, while say is the Looks block for on-screen text. Treating them as the same would lead to answers that confuse how sprites communicate in a game or a simulation.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Draw or describe the block sequence for two sprites in a cricket match: a bowler and a batsman. The bowler should run up, wait, and then `broadcast bowl`. The batsman should hit the ball when it receives the message. Explain the order of events.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: In the cricket project, the bowler sprite starts with `when green flag clicked`. Under that event, place a few motion blocks, such as `go to x:-150 y:-50`, then a short loop to make the bowler run toward the pitch, followed by a `wait 1 secs` block so the action does not happen too quickly, and finally a `broadcast bowl` block with the message name `bowl`. The script then ends, but the message has already been sent to every sprite and the stage. The batsman sprite has its own independent script starting with `when I receive bowl`. Under that event, the batsman can first `go to x:50 y:-40`, then `switch costume to bat-swing`, then `change x by 20` to show the swing, and finally `say "It's a six!" for 2 seconds`. The key is that the bowler does not know what the batsman does; it simply shouts the message `bowl`. The batsman decides to react because it has the matching receive hat. The wait block inside the bowler's script gives the player time to see the run-up before the message is sent. If the batsman's receive hat were missing or the message name were misspelled, the batsman would not move, which is why the message name must be exactly the same in both places.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a traffic-light simulation for a crossing in an Indian city. Explain how the four control blocks can work together so that cars stop at red and go at green, and so that a second road sprite knows when the light has changed.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: My simulation is for a busy crossing in Mumbai. The first sprite is the traffic light, and the second sprite is a car. I start the traffic-light script with `when green flag clicked`. I then use a `forever` block because the light must keep cycling forever. Inside the forever, I first `switch costume to green light` and `wait 5 secs`, then `switch costume to yellow light` and `wait 2 secs`, then `switch costume to red light` and `wait 5 secs`. To tell the car what is happening, I add a `broadcast red now` before the red light wait and a `broadcast green now` before the green light wait. The car sprite has two scripts: `when I receive red now` makes the car `glide to x:60 y:-100 in 2 secs` to stop, and `when I receive green now` makes the car `glide to x:300 y:-100 in 3 secs` to move forward. I also use an `if-then` block in the car script when it touches the stop line, so that if the light is red the car says "Waiting!" before it moves. In this way the forever block runs the light cycle continuously, the wait blocks create realistic delays, the if-then checks a condition, and the broadcast blocks coordinate between the traffic light and the car. This is a complete example of how control blocks manage the flow of a simple game or simulation.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to identify the forever, if-then, wait, and broadcast blocks as members of the Control category and explain in their own words what each one does to program flow — repeat without stopping, choose based on a true/false condition, pause one script for a fixed number of seconds, and send a named message to all sprites and the stage. The student must also be able to assemble these blocks correctly in a Scratch script: place a forever block under an event hat with motion and looks blocks nested inside it, snap a hexagonal condition block into the mouth of an if-then, build a forever-if combination that checks a condition every cycle, and pair a broadcast block with a matching `when I receive` hat on another sprite. Finally, the student must be able to combine two or more of these blocks in a single short project, such as a traffic light or a two-sprite cricket scene, and justify in one or two sentences why each control block is needed.

title: Scratch variables and operators - data, sensing, operators blocks
subject: cs
definition:
In Scratch, a variable is a named container that can store a value and change while a program runs. Think of it as a small labelled box inside the computer’s memory: you can put a number in it, look at what is inside, and replace or update that number whenever you want. The word data simply means the information the program is working with, and a variable is how Scratch keeps track of data such as a score, a player’s health, or the number of collected coins. To make a variable, you use the "Make a Variable" button in the Data section of the blocks palette, give the variable a meaningful name such as "score", decide whether it is for one sprite only or for all sprites, and Scratch creates special blocks that let you set, change, and show the value on the stage. The score is one of the most common classroom examples because it starts at zero and increases or decreases as the player does things in a game.

Operator blocks are the arithmetic and logic tools in Scratch. They live in the Operators section and include blocks for add, subtract, multiply, and divide, as well as blocks that compare two values, such as greater than, less than, or equal to. These comparison operators are important because they produce a true or false answer that can be fed into an if-then block or a repeat-until block. For example, if score > 10 then say "You win!" uses an operator inside a control block. An operator in Scratch works much like a calculator: you place numbers or variables into its blank spaces, and it returns the result. The result can then be stored back in a variable, used in a movement command, or checked in a condition.

Sensing blocks allow a sprite to detect what is happening on the stage, with the computer, or with the user. The touching block can check whether a sprite is touching another sprite or a particular colour. The key pressed block checks whether a key such as the space bar, the up arrow, or a letter key is being pressed. Mouse position blocks report where the mouse pointer is on the stage. When these sensing blocks are placed inside control blocks, they become the eyes and ears of a game. A simple platform game might use touching to decide whether a player sprite has touched a coin, key pressed to move the player left or right, and a variable called score to remember how many coins have been collected. Together, variables store data, operators compute and compare values, and sensing blocks read the world, allowing a Scratch project to behave like an interactive game.
eli5: A variable is like a jar with a label. You can put a number inside and change it later. A score variable keeps count of points. Operators are like little calculators that add, subtract, or compare numbers. Sensing blocks are like eyes and ears that check whether a sprite is touching something or a key is pressed. Together they help you make a game that moves, counts, and reacts.

misconceptions.belief: Students often give variables the wrong name or use the same name for different things. CISCE examiners have noticed that candidates "did not write the same class name or variable names as mentioned in the question." In Scratch this means a student might call the variable "Score" in one place and "score" in another, or use a name like "x" that does not describe the data.
misconceptions.correction: choose one clear, meaningful name and use it everywhere. Write "score" and spell it exactly the same each time.

misconceptions.belief: Students confuse arithmetic and comparison operators, or write the wrong symbol. The examiners pointed out that candidates were "not having written the syntax of relational operators properly." In Scratch, a green operator block with two blank spaces and a drop-down arrow must be set to the right comparison such as greater than, less than, or equal to. A weak project might place an add block where a compare block is needed, or choose the wrong comparison.
misconceptions.correction: ask what the block must answer. If the answer is a number, use an arithmetic operator. If the answer is true or false for a decision, use a comparison operator.

misconceptions.belief: Students forget to initialise variables before using them. CISCE examiners have written that candidates did not "declare the member variables" or did not "accept the variables" correctly. In Scratch terms, this means a student might use the "change score by 1" block without first setting "score" to 0 when the green flag is clicked, so the score starts at nothing or a random value.
misconceptions.correction: always begin the game with a "set score to 0" or similar block under the "when green flag clicked" hat, before any other script changes the variable.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What is a variable in Scratch, and what is the purpose of the "change score by 1" block?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A variable in Scratch is a named storage area that can hold a value and have that value updated while the program is running. It is created in the Data section of the blocks palette by clicking "Make a Variable," giving it a name such as "score," and deciding whether it is for the current sprite only or for all sprites. Once the variable is made, Scratch creates several blocks including "set score to ..." and "change score by ..." The purpose of the "change score by 1" block is to increase the current value stored in the score variable by one. This is useful in games because every time a player sprite touches a coin, fruit, or target, the score can be updated automatically. The block does not replace the old value; it adds to it. If the score is 5 and the block runs, the score becomes 6. This is why a variable is different from a constant value written directly in a script: it remembers and grows.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student wants a bird sprite to flap its wings and move up when the space bar is pressed. Explain which blocks and operators the student should use and why.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student should start with a "when green flag clicked" hat block from the Events section and a "forever" block from the Control section to keep checking for input. Inside the forever loop, place an if-then block. The condition for the if-then block should come from the Sensing section: a "key space pressed?" block, which reports true when the space bar is held down and false otherwise. Inside the if-then block, the student needs the bird to move upward. That can be done with a Motion block such as "change y by 10," where the positive number moves the sprite upward. If the bird should also play a flap sound, an "play sound" block can be added. An operator is not strictly needed here, but one could be used to set a speed. For example, a variable called "speed" could be set to 10, and "change y by speed" could use the value stored in the variable. The reason this combination works is that the sensing block reads the keyboard, the control block makes the decision, the motion block carries out the action, and the variable stores any changing data such as speed or height.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A classmate says, "Using many variables makes a Scratch project better, so I should create a variable for every small thing in my game." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is only partly true. Variables are very useful for storing and updating data, but creating too many of them can make a project harder to read, test, and fix. A good Scratch game should use variables for real purposes: a score that changes, a timer that counts down, a speed that increases, or a health value that decreases. These are meaningful pieces of data that affect how the game behaves. If a student creates a variable for every tiny detail, such as one variable for the x-position of a sprite that already has an x-position reporter built into Scratch, the extra variable is unnecessary and can cause confusion. Unnecessary variables also waste memory and increase the chance of mistakes, because the student must remember to set and update each one. On the other hand, too few variables can also be a problem. For example, a game with no score variable cannot remember how many points the player has earned, and a game with no speed variable cannot make enemies move faster over time. Therefore, the balanced view is to use enough variables to store the data that truly changes and matters, but not so many that the project becomes crowded. A well-planned game might use just three or four clearly named variables: score, lives, time, and level. This keeps the project organised while still allowing rich, changing behaviour.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple collecting game where a basket sprite catches falling apples. The score must increase by one each time an apple is caught. Write the main scripts for the basket and the apples, including variables and sensing blocks.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First create a variable called "score" for all sprites. When the green flag is clicked, set score to 0. For the basket sprite, place a "when green flag clicked" hat, add a "forever" loop, and inside the loop place an if-then block with the condition "key right arrow pressed?" from the Sensing section. Inside that if-then, add "change x by 10." Add another if-then for the left arrow with "change x by -10." This lets the player move the basket. For the apples, create several clones or one apple that falls repeatedly. When the game starts, set the apple's y position to the top of the stage and pick a random x position. Use a forever or repeat-until loop to keep moving the apple downward with "change y by -5" until it reaches the bottom. To increase the score, use an if-then block that checks whether the apple is "touching basket?" from the Sensing section. If true, play a short sound, use the operator block "change score by 1" from the Data section, and reset the apple to the top with a new random x position. The comparison and sensing blocks work together: the touching block detects the catch, and the change block updates the score. The arithmetic operator is the hidden "+1" inside the "change score by" block, and the score variable keeps the running total from one catch to the next.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Imagine you have been asked to improve the collecting game by adding a timer and a win condition. Describe how you would use variables, operators, and sensing blocks to create a 30-second challenge where the player wins if the score reaches 10 before time runs out.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would add two more variables: "time" and "game over." When the green flag is clicked, I would set score to 0, set time to 30, and set game over to 0. I would create a separate script that starts with a "when green flag clicked" hat and uses a "repeat until" block. The condition inside the repeat until would use a comparison operator to check whether time equals 0 or game over equals 1. Inside the repeat, wait one second, then use the "change time by -1" block. This counts the timer down every second. In the basket and apple scripts, when an apple is caught, I would first change score by 1, then add an if-then block that uses a comparison operator to check whether score is greater than or equal to 10. If that is true, I would set game over to 1, broadcast a "win" message, and make the sprite say "You win!" Using game over set to 1 makes the timer loop stop, and it also tells all other scripts to stop moving. If the time reaches 0 before the score reaches 10, the repeat until loop ends on its own, and I would broadcast a "lose" message so the sprite can say "Try again!" This design uses variables for score, time, and game over, operators to subtract from the timer and compare the score to 10, and sensing blocks to detect when the apple touches the basket. The result is a complete, timed game with a clear win condition.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to create a named variable in Scratch using the "Make a Variable" option in the Data section, initialise it with a "set ... to ..." block under the "when green flag clicked" hat, and update it correctly with the "change ... by ..." block inside an if-then or forever block. The student must also be able to choose the correct operator block for a given purpose, distinguishing arithmetic operators (add, subtract, multiply, divide) that return a number from comparison operators (greater than, less than, equal to) that return true or false, and place the comparison operator inside an if-then or repeat-until condition. Finally, the student must be able to select and use the right sensing block, such as "touching ...", "key ... pressed?", or "mouse x / mouse y", to detect collisions, keyboard input, or mouse position, and explain how the true or false result from that sensing block drives a decision in a control block.

title: Creating a simple game in Scratch - movement, collision, scoring
subject: cs
definition:
Creating a simple game in Scratch is the process of programming an interactive animation in which a player sprite responds to input, checks for contact with a target sprite, and updates a numeric score. At its heart, the activity brings together three separate ideas: movement, collision, and scoring. Movement is produced by sensing blocks that wait for the arrow keys to be pressed, then by motion blocks that change the player sprite’s x or y position. Collision occurs when the player sprite comes close enough to the target sprite to touch it, and the touching sensor reports true. Scoring is a variable that starts at zero and is increased each time a collision is detected. To keep everything running, the entire logic is placed inside a game loop, usually a forever or repeat until block, so the program keeps checking for key presses and collisions as long as the game is active.

A well-known example is a catch game. A child in India might design a game in which a basket (the player) is moved left and right with the left and right arrow keys to catch falling fruits (the target). When the basket touches a fruit, the target is hidden, the score is increased by one, and the fruit reappears at a new random position. This requires event blocks to start the game, control blocks to repeat the checks, and operator blocks to decide whether the touching condition is true. The variable Score is created in the Data category, set to 0 when the green flag is clicked, and increased using the change Score by 1 block inside an if-then block. Without the sensing block that detects the arrow keys, the player cannot move; without the touching sensor, the sprite cannot detect a collision; and without the variable, there can be no scoring. Good Scratch game design, therefore, is not about using one block at a time, but about combining motion, sensing, control, and data blocks into one complete script. The result is a simple game that a Class 6 student can explain, modify, and demonstrate to peers.
eli5: A Scratch game is like playing catch with your computer. You move a player sprite with the arrow keys, and when it touches the target, the computer adds one point to your score. A forever loop makes the game keep checking your keys and the touching again and again, so the game never stops until you say so.

diagnosticQuestions.question: List the four types of Scratch blocks used to create a simple game with movement, collision, and scoring, and give one example of each.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A simple Scratch game uses four kinds of blocks: motion, sensing, control, and data. Motion blocks move the player sprite: for example, change x by 10 moves the sprite to the right when the right arrow key is pressed. Sensing blocks detect input and contact: the key pressed? block checks whether an arrow key is down, and the touching mouse-pointer? or touching sprite2? block reports a collision between the player and the target. Control blocks manage the order and repetition: the when green flag clicked hat starts the game, and the forever loop keeps the script running so the player can keep moving and the target can keep checking for contact. Data blocks store the score: a variable named Score is created, set to 0 at the start, and updated with change Score by 1 each time the player catches the target. Without these four kinds of blocks, the game cannot combine movement, collision, and scoring into one working program. In the board answer, simply naming the blocks is not enough; you must also say what each one does in the game.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is it important to place the scoring command inside an if-then block rather than directly inside the forever loop?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The scoring command must run only when the player actually catches the target. If the change Score by 1 block were placed directly inside the forever loop without an if-then condition, the score would increase every time the loop repeats, even when the player is far away from the target. This would make the score meaningless because it would climb rapidly without any real collision. The if-then block acts like a guard: it first asks the sensing question, “Is the player touching the target?” If the answer is true, the script inside the if-then runs and the score goes up by one. If the answer is false, the script skips the scoring step and the loop continues. This separation of detection and action is what makes the game fair. In the board exam, students who lose marks often forget this guard and put the variable change outside the condition, so their game “scores” continuously. The correct structure is therefore forever → if touching then → change score. You should also remember to set Score to 0 before the loop, so the count begins from the first catch and not from a random number.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says: “I do not need a game loop; I can put all the arrow-key scripts under separate when key pressed hats and put the collision check under a when this sprite clicked hat. This will make the program shorter and faster.” Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer:
There is some truth in the student’s idea, but it is not the best design for this kind of game. Using separate when key pressed hats for each arrow is indeed a valid way to move the player, and it can make the scripts look shorter because each hat has only one motion command. However, the collision check cannot be safely placed under a one-time event such as when this sprite clicked, because a catch game needs the target to keep testing for contact as the player moves. If the check runs only when the sprite is clicked, the score will update once at the start and then never again, no matter how many times the player touches the target.

A game loop is not extra code; it is the heart of the game. The forever block repeats the key and touching checks many times every second, giving the player a smooth, continuous experience. If the arrow keys are also handled inside the same forever loop using key pressed? blocks, the teacher can see one complete script that shows motion, sensing, control, and variables together. This is exactly what the ICSE/ISC practical wants: the ability to combine all four block types into a complete game.

The only situation where the student’s shorter approach could work is for a game that scores only once, such as clicking a “win” button. But for a catch game with a moving target and a changing score, the loop is necessary. Therefore, the statement is partly correct about movement but incorrect about collision and scoring. The better choice is to keep the arrow-key and touching logic inside a forever loop so that the game is continuous, responsive, and fair.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a Scratch game called “Ganga Cleanup” in which a boat (player) moves left and right with arrow keys and catches floating plastic bottles (target). Write the main scripts for the boat and the bottle, and explain how the score changes.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: In Ganga Cleanup, the stage shows a river background. The boat is the player and the plastic bottle is the target. When the green flag is clicked, the boat goes to the bottom center of the stage and the bottle is placed at a random x position at the top. Inside a forever loop on the boat, the script checks the left and right arrow keys: if key left arrow pressed? then change x by -10, and if key right arrow pressed? then change x by 10. On the bottle, a second forever loop moves it down by 5 steps each cycle and checks whether it is touching the boat. If it is touching, the score should increase by 1, the bottle should hide, wait a moment, then move to a new random x at the top and show again. The score variable is created in the Data category and set to 0 at the start. This combines movement, collision detection, and scoring exactly as the node describes. The Indian example also helps to remember that a game can be about real-life problems such as cleaning a river. In your board script, do not forget the game loop, because without it the bottle will fall only once and the score will not update after the first catch.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Invent a new two-level Scratch game and describe the blocks that would make it work. Your game should use at least one player, one target, and a score.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: My game is called “Spice Market Dash.” Level 1 is set on a busy Indian street. The player is a delivery scooter that moves with the arrow keys to catch falling spice boxes. The target is a spice box that falls from random positions at the top. Each catch adds 1 to the Score variable. After five catches, the game announces “Level 2” using a looks say block and changes the background to a railway station. Level 2 adds two spice boxes falling at the same time, so the player must catch either box. The score continues from Level 1. The scripts use when green flag clicked to start, forever loops to move the boxes and check for touching, and if-then blocks inside the loops to decide when to increase the score. An operator block can also check whether Score is greater than 5 to trigger the level change. This shows that a simple game can be extended by adding more targets and using variables for both score and level. The two levels prove that a student can move beyond copying the textbook example and design something original for the practical exam.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to assemble a complete, runnable Scratch game script that combines movement (using key pressed? sensing blocks with change x by / change y by motion blocks inside a forever loop), collision detection (using the touching sensor inside an if-then block nested in the same or a parallel forever loop), and scoring (a variable created in the Data category, set to 0 on green flag, and updated with change Score by 1 only when the touching condition is true). The student must also be able to explain, in their own words, why the game loop, the if-then guard, and the change-by operator (rather than set-to) are each necessary for the game to work fairly and continuously. Finally, the student must be able to design an original Indian-context game (such as a boat catching plastic bottles on the Ganga or a bat catching a cricket ball) and write out the boat/player and target scripts from memory, not merely copy the textbook example.

title: HTML introduction - structure, tags, elements, creating a web page
subject: cs
definition:
HTML, which stands for HyperText Markup Language, is the standard language used to create and structure a web page. It is not a programming language in the sense that it does not tell the computer how to calculate or make decisions; instead, it is a markup language because it tells a browser how to organise and display text, images and other content. Every instruction in HTML is given through a tag. A tag is a special word placed inside angle brackets, such as <html>, <head>, <body> and <title>. Tags usually appear in pairs: an opening tag that marks the beginning of an instruction and a closing tag that marks the end. The closing tag looks the same as the opening tag but contains a forward slash before the keyword, as in </title>. The opening tag, the closing tag and the content placed between them together form an element. The element is therefore the complete unit that the browser can interpret and display.

The structure of an HTML document is always nested in a clear, logical order. The whole page is wrapped inside the <html> element, which acts as the outer container or the frame of the document. Inside the <html> element there are two main sections: the <head> section and the <body> section. The <head> section holds information about the page that is not directly visible on the web page itself, such as the <title>, which is the text that appears on the browser’s title bar or tab. The <body> section holds everything the reader can actually see when the page is opened, including headings, paragraphs, images, links and other visible content. Because these elements fit inside one another like a set of boxes, the closing of tags must follow the rule of last opened, first closed. If an opening tag is placed before another, its closing tag must come after the inner tag has been closed.

Creating a basic HTML document is a simple practical skill. A learner can type the HTML code into any plain text editor, such as Notepad on Windows, and must then save the file with the .html extension. The .html extension is important because it tells the operating system and the browser that the file should be treated as a web page and not as an ordinary text document. Once the file is saved, it can be opened in any web browser. The browser reads the tags, interprets their meaning and renders the page for the user. Writing a simple HTML page that contains a title, a heading and a paragraph, saving it correctly and viewing it in a browser is the first practical step in the larger spiral topic of web development that continues with advanced HTML and other web technologies in later classes.

It is a bit like putting a letter inside an envelope before sending it.

In HTML this appears as writing [title] or (html) instead of <title> and <html>. The correction is that HTML tags must always be written inside angle brackets, and the closing tag must include a forward slash before the keyword, as in </title>.

Some learners do not understand the idea of nesting and close tags in the wrong order, similar to the examiner observation that candidates had "difficulty in moving the pointer to the next node and in checking for the null condition." In HTML this becomes <html><head></html></head>, which is wrong because the inner tag must be closed before the outer tag. The correction is to remember that the last tag opened must be the first tag closed, so <html> is opened first and closed last.

The correction is to always save the file with the .html extension and then open it in a browser to see the actual web page.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What does HTML stand for? Name the four main structural tags and explain the purpose of each.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language, and it is the standard language used to create a web page. The four main structural tags are <html>, <head>, <body> and <title>. The <html> tag is the outer container that wraps everything in the document, telling the browser that the file is an HTML page. The <head> tag contains information about the page that is not visible on the page itself, such as the <title> and any special instructions. The <title> tag, placed inside the <head>, sets the text that appears on the browser tab or title bar. The <body> tag contains all the visible content of the page, such as headings, paragraphs, images and links, that the user sees and reads. These four tags work together to give the web page a clear structure. Without them the browser would not know which part of the document is the page name and which part is the visible content.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why must the <title> tag be placed inside the <head> section and not inside the <body> section?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The <title> tag must be placed inside the <head> section because the head is the part of the HTML document that holds information about the page rather than the visible page content. The title is not meant to appear as a heading or paragraph on the web page itself; instead, it is meant to appear on the browser tab or title bar, which is information about the page. If the <title> tag were placed inside the <body> section, the browser might still read it, but it would not appear on the tab in the correct way, and the structure of the document would be wrong. The <body> section should only contain the content that the reader is meant to see, such as a main heading and a paragraph. Keeping the title inside the <head> also helps the browser understand the page before it begins rendering the visible parts, which is why the head comes before the body. This clean separation between information about the page and the visible content is one of the most important rules in HTML.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "When I write <title>About India</title>, the words About India will appear as a heading on the web page itself." Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The statement is mostly incorrect, although it contains one important truth. The truth is that the text between and is indeed a meaningful piece of content, but it is not displayed on the web page itself. Instead, the title text appears on the browser tab or in the title bar, which is part of the browser window and not the rendered page. The student has confused the element with a heading element such as <h1>. A heading tag like <h1>About India</h1> placed inside the <body> section would appear as a large heading on the actual page. The <title> tag, however, is always placed inside the <head> section and provides information about the page rather than visible page content. On the one hand, the statement shows that the student understands that HTML tags contain text, which is a good starting point. On the other hand, the student has not yet grasped the difference between the head and the body, and between a page title and a visible heading. Therefore, the statement should be corrected by explaining that <title> is for the browser tab and <h1> or another heading tag is for the visible heading, and that the title tag belongs in the head, not the body.

title: HTML attributes and background - bgcolor, text color, font
subject: cs
definition:
HTML, or HyperText Markup Language, is the language we use to build the structure and appearance of a web page. In this node, we focus on the idea of an attribute, which is an extra piece of information placed inside the opening tag of an HTML element to modify its behaviour or appearance. An attribute is always written as a name-value pair, such as name="value", and it sits after the tag name but before the closing angle bracket. We have already met attributes when we used img src to tell the browser which image to show and a href to tell the browser where a link should go. Now we extend the same idea to the body tag and the font tag to control the look of a page.

The body tag encloses everything that appears in the browser window. By adding the bgcolor attribute inside the body tag, we can set the background colour of the entire page. For example, <body bgcolor="yellow"> paints the whole page yellow, just as we might change the wallpaper on the desktop of a computer. The value of the attribute can be a colour name such as "red", "blue", "green", "white" or "black", or a hexadecimal colour code such as "#FF0000" for red. The text attribute of the body tag changes the default colour of all text on the page. If we write <body bgcolor="black" text="white">, the page will have a black background and all ordinary text will appear in white unless a smaller tag overrides it.

The font tag is used to change the appearance of a selected piece of text. It has three important attributes: face, size and color. The face attribute sets the font family, such as "Arial", "Times New Roman" or "Courier New". The size attribute takes a number from 1 to 7, where 1 is the smallest and 7 is the largest. The color attribute sets the colour of the text between the opening <font> and the closing </font> tags. A typical use would be <font face="Arial" size="4" color="blue">Welcome to India</font>. This tag is useful for styling headings, names of places, or important words inside a paragraph, but it should not be placed in the body tag itself because it is meant for individual pieces of text. When the browser reads the page, it first applies the body-level attributes, then the font-level attributes, so a local font colour will override the global text colour for that small section.

The body tag's bgcolor attribute paints the whole page background, the text attribute picks the usual writing colour, and the font tag changes the look of a few chosen words using face, size and color. It is just like painting a room and then choosing different pens for the special words you want to stand out.

diagnosticQuestions.answer: The font tag is used to style a selected portion of text and it has three main attributes: face, size and color. The face attribute sets the font family, for example "Arial" or "Times New Roman". The size attribute takes a number from 1 to 7, where 1 is the smallest and 7 is the largest. The color attribute sets the colour of the text between the opening <font> and the closing </font> tags. The body tag, which holds the visible part of the web page, uses the bgcolor attribute to set the background colour of the entire page and the text attribute to set the default colour of all text that is not specifically styled by another tag such as font. These five pieces of information are the core facts the node expects you to remember.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why does the font tag have a closing tag </font>, while the body tag does not need a separate closing instruction for the bgcolor and text attributes to take effect?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The font tag controls only a small piece of text, so it needs an opening tag to mark where the special style begins and a closing tag </font> to mark where the style stops. Without the closing tag, the browser continues to apply the chosen face, size and colour to every word that follows, which can change the whole page. In contrast, the body tag uses attributes to describe one overall setting for the entire page. The bgcolor and text attributes are placed inside the single opening <body> tag, and they take effect for the whole page from the moment the tag is opened until the body ends at </body>. There is no need for a separate closing of the attribute because the attribute is not a container; it is a modifier that applies across the entire section it lives in. This shows that attributes inside body are global, while the font tag with attributes is local.

An HTML table is a structured arrangement of information into horizontal rows and vertical columns, created by nesting a set of four core tags inside an HTML document. The tag acts as the outer container — it tells the browser that everything placed inside it should be treated as one table. Inside the

The days and period names should be placed in cells because they describe the data, while the actual lesson details go into cells. To make the grid lines visible, the tag is given the border attribute, as in

Tables are useful whenever information is naturally two-dimensional: a marksheet can show student names in one column and their marks in another, a bus schedule from Chennai to Bengaluru can show departure and arrival times, and a shopping bill can list items, quantities and prices side by side. Correct nesting is essential: a 		or cannot sit directly inside a ; it must first be wrapped by a , just as a chapter must come inside a book before you can place sentences inside it. eli5: Imagine your marksheet drawn on paper with rows and columns. In HTML, the <table> tag is the whole sheet, <tr> is each horizontal line, <td> is each ordinary box, and <th> is the bold heading box. The border attribute is like drawing lines around every box so you can see the grid clearly. When you write the tags in the right order, the browser draws a neat table for you.

It is meant for the titles that describe the rows or the columns, such as "Day", "Subject" or "Marks". A browser usually displays the text inside a tag in bold and in the centre of the cell, which makes the headings stand out. When these four tags are used together in the correct order, the browser can draw a neat grid on the page. For example, in a timetable for a school in Kolkata, "Monday" and "Tuesday" might sit in cells, while "Mathematics" and "English" sit in cells. The tags therefore have different jobs, and using the right one makes the table both correct and easy to read.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why must <td> or <th> tags always be written inside <tr> tags, and why is it important to use <th> for the first row of a marksheet instead of using <td> for every cell?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A table is built as a hierarchy, not as a flat list. The <table> tag is the top container; the <tr> tag is the next level down, and it represents one horizontal row. Inside each <tr>, the <td> or <th> tags are the smallest units, the actual cells. The cells cannot float directly inside the <table> tag because the browser needs to know how many horizontal lines the table has and how many boxes are in each line. That is why every <td> or <th> must be placed inside a <tr> tag. If you leave out the <tr>, the browser has no row to put the cell into, and the table will not display as a proper grid. The reason for using <th> in the first row is that the first row usually contains the column titles. A header cell is bold and centred, so the reader can immediately see that "Subject" and "Marks" are labels, not data. If you use <td> for every cell, the headings look the same as the marks, and the table becomes harder to understand. In a marksheet for a school in Bengaluru, for example, the first row should contain <th> cells for "Roll Number", "Name", "English", "Mathematics" and "Science", while the rest of the rows should contain <td> cells for the actual roll numbers, names and marks. This distinction shows the examiner that the student knows the difference between a label and a value.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student says, "We can use <td> for both headings and data in a table. Using <th> is just an extra tag that does not matter, because the browser will show the table anyway." Do you agree? Give a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: On the surface, the student's statement has some truth in it. If you write a table and put everything inside <td> tags, the browser will indeed show the table. The grid will appear, and the data will be visible. For this reason, some beginners think that <th> is unnecessary and that <td> can do the whole job. However, this view is only partly correct. The <th> tag is not an extra tag that does nothing; it has an important purpose. When the browser sees a <th> tag, it automatically makes the text bold and centred, which helps the reader to recognise that this cell is a heading, not a data value. More importantly, the choice between <td> and <th> carries meaning. A table with proper <th> tags tells both the browser and the human reader which rows or columns are being described. In the ICSE board examination, the examiner looks for this understanding. Using <td> for headings may still produce a visible table, but it shows that the student has not understood the difference between a header cell and a data cell, and marks can be lost for that. On the other hand, the student is right that the table will still be displayed, so the mistake is not as serious as missing the <table> or <tr> tags. The balanced answer is that a table made only with <td> tags is technically possible and visible, but it is not good HTML practice. For a proper marksheet, timetable or schedule, the headings should always be marked with <th>, and the data should be marked with <td>. This makes the table clearer, more meaningful and more likely to gain full marks.

title: HTML forms - form, input, text, radio, checkbox, submit
subject: cs
definition: An HTML form is a special container built with the <form> ... </form> tag that turns a silent web page into an interactive conversation. Inside the form tag we place one or more input elements using the empty <input> tag. The behaviour of each input is controlled by its type attribute, so the same <input> tag can become a text box, a radio button, a checkbox, or a submit button depending on the value of type. When type="text", the browser shows a single-line blank space where a visitor can type information such as a name, city, or email address. When a group of inputs are given type="radio", the browser treats them as a single-choice set: the user may pick exactly one option, just as a multiple-choice question allows only one answer. To make radio buttons work as a set, every input in that set must share the same name attribute; the value attribute of the chosen one is sent with the form data. When type="checkbox", each box stands independently and the user may tick none, one, or many of them, which is why checkboxes are ideal for collecting multiple interests or a list of items. Finally, type="submit" creates a button that sends, or submits, the collected information to a web server or to an email program. A form may also contain ordinary HTML content such as headings, paragraphs, and bold labels, so it is not a strange new world but an extension of what the learner already knows about structured web pages. In the ICSE syllabus the forms chapter is expected to be applied to real tasks: a simple registration page for an online school event in New Delhi, a feedback page for a trip to a science centre in Bangalore, or a contact page for a local club in Mumbai. Indian examples such as the IRCTC passenger details page, the National Portal of India feedback forms, or a school website’s admission page all use the same four input types. The important vocabulary for this node includes form, input, text, radio, checkbox, submit, button, type, name, value, and interactive. Understanding these terms lets a student build pages that collect information rather than only display it.
eli5: A form is like a paper form on a screen. The <form> tag is the page that holds all the blank boxes. You can type in a text box, pick one answer with a radio button, tick many boxes with checkboxes, and press the submit button to send your answers.

misconceptions.belief: Many learners treat the name and value attributes as the same thing, or they forget the type attribute entirely. This is similar to the CISCE PPA 2024 comment that many candidates were confused between complement and dual because the two ideas look related. In a form, type tells the browser what to show, name identifies the field, and value is the actual answer. The correction is to use type="radio" name="Gender" value="Girl" so the browser, the server, and the human reader all know what each part means.

Some students create only one <input> tag for a whole set of options, or they give every radio button a different name. This matches the CISCE PPA 2024 remark that some candidates used a single input for the OR and NOR gates or drew an 8x1 multiplexer with extra selection lines. In HTML, every radio option needs its own <input> tag, but all options in the same set must share the same name. If the names differ, the user can select more than one option and the form stops behaving like a multiple-choice question.

Learners often think that radio and checkbox are just different shapes and can be swapped freely. The CISCE PPA 2019 observations show that students sometimes apply a rule from one topic to another without checking the underlying definition, and the remedy given was to review topic fundamentals. Radio buttons are exclusive because the name attribute groups them into one set, so the user can pick only one. Checkboxes are independent, so the user may tick several. The correction is to ask, “Do I want one answer or many answers?” before choosing the input type.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the <form> tag in an HTML document, and why must input elements be placed inside it?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The <form> tag is the container that turns a collection of input fields into a single unit that the browser can submit. It tells the browser that all the input elements inside it belong together and that their data should be gathered when the user presses the submit button. Without the form tag, the input elements would still appear on the page, but the browser would not know that they are part of a single questionnaire. The form tag also usually has an action attribute that says where the data should be sent, although at Class 7 the focus is mainly on creating the visible form. Inside the form tag, the text, radio, checkbox, and submit inputs are nested just as headings and paragraphs were nested inside the <body> tag in earlier chapters. For example, a form for a feedback page in New Delhi could begin with <form action="...">, contain an h2 heading, a paragraph, and several input tags, and close with </form>. This container idea is the same concept the learner met in c7_cs_021, where one tag wraps related content.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why must all the radio buttons in one set have the same name attribute, and what happens if each radio button has a different name?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The name attribute is the invisible label that groups radio buttons together. When several radio inputs share the same name, the browser treats them as one multiple-choice set and makes them mutually exclusive, which means selecting one automatically removes the selection from the others. The value attribute of the chosen button is the actual answer that the form sends. If each radio button is given a different name, such as name="OptionA", name="OptionB", and name="OptionC", the browser sees them as three separate questions rather than one question with three options. Then the user can click all three at the same time, which destroys the single-choice behaviour. A correctly designed set uses the same name and different values, for example <input type="radio" name="City" value="Delhi">, <input type="radio" name="City" value="Mumbai">, and <input type="radio" name="City" value="Chennai">. This is one of the most important details the examiner will look for in a Class 7 form.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student claims, “Radio buttons and checkboxes are exactly the same except for their shape, so I can use them interchangeably when designing a form.” Evaluate this statement.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is not correct, because the two input types have different rules of behaviour that depend on the name attribute and on what the question is trying to collect. Radio buttons are used when only one option can be selected from a group, such as choosing one age group, one city, or one answer in a multiple-choice question. They become exclusive because all radio inputs in the set share the same name. Checkboxes, on the other hand, are used when the user may choose any number of options from a list, such as selecting multiple hobbies, multiple subjects, or multiple help tasks. Each checkbox is independent, so it can be selected or deselected without affecting the others. It is true that both appear as small boxes next to labels and both use the <input> tag, but that surface similarity hides the different purpose. In some special cases a form may contain only two radio buttons for a simple yes or no answer, or only one checkbox for a single terms-and-conditions tick, but even then the rule remains: one answer means radio, and zero or more answers means checkbox. Therefore, the student’s claim confuses appearance with function and would lead to forms that collect wrong information.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a simple HTML registration form for a school science fair in Bangalore. The form must include a text field for the student’s name, a radio group to choose one project type, two or more checkboxes to choose the days the student can attend, and a submit button. Write the HTML code and explain how each part works.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The HTML for the registration page could look like this. First, the <form> tag is opened and closed to hold everything. An h2 heading “Bangalore School Science Fair Registration” and a short paragraph give the user instructions. The text input is <input type="text" name="StudentName" placeholder="Enter your name">, which creates a single-line box for the student’s name. The radio group uses the same name, so <input type="radio" name="ProjectType" value="Model"> Model, <input type="radio" name="ProjectType" value="Chart"> Chart, and <input type="radio" name="ProjectType" value="Experiment"> Experiment make the student choose only one project type. The attendance checkboxes are <input type="checkbox" name="Day" value="Monday"> Monday, <input type="checkbox" name="Day" value="Wednesday"> Wednesday, and <input type="checkbox" name="Day" value="Friday"> Friday, allowing the student to tick one or more days. Finally, <input type="submit" value="Register Now"> sends all the chosen information to the server. The name attributes ensure the server can read each piece of data, the value attributes tell the server what was chosen, and the type attributes decide whether the user types, selects one, selects many, or presses a button. The form is a clear, working example of the ICSE Class 7 form objectives.

The feedback page should begin with the title “National Museum Visitor Feedback — New Delhi” inside an h2 tag and a short paragraph thanking the visitor. The form tag wraps the whole questionnaire. At the top, a text input asks for the visitor’s name:

After that, three checkboxes collect the facilities used, each with the name “Facility” but with different values: Audio Guide, Museum Cafe, and Souvenir Shop. At the bottom, creates the button that submits the form. The layout can be a simple vertical list with a label before each input, making it easy for a visitor on a phone or computer. This form uses all four required input types and shows the difference between one-choice radio and many-choice checkboxes in a real Indian setting.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to write a complete, correctly nested HTML form that uses the <form> container and at least the four input types covered in this node: type="text" for a single-line entry, type="radio" for a single-choice set with a shared name attribute, type="checkbox" for an independent multi-select list, and type="submit" for a working submit button. The student must also be able to choose correctly between radio and checkbox for a given real-life question (one answer versus many answers) and must justify that choice by referring to the name and value attributes rather than to the visual shape of the control. Finally, the student must be able to spot and correct a faulty form in which radio buttons have different names, a checkbox set has only one option or repeated values, or the submit control is replaced by plain text or a non-submit button.

title: Scratch custom blocks and clones - procedures and duplication
subject: cs
definition:
Scratch is a block-based programming language where learners build programs by snapping colourful code blocks together. As projects grow larger, scripts can become long and repetitive. The two powerful ideas in this node — custom blocks and clones — help a programmer keep scripts tidy and create lively animations or games. A **custom block** is a new, user-made **command** that groups a sequence of actions under a single, friendly name. Once defined, it can be called again and again, just like saying a short code word for a longer sentence. The collection of steps inside a custom block is called a **procedure**. A **parameter** is a special input that lets the same block behave differently each time it is used; for example, a custom block named `moveSquare` could accept a parameter called `side` so the sprite draws a small or large square depending on the value supplied. This ability makes the project more flexible because one definition works for many cases.
A **clone** is a runtime **duplicate** of a sprite. Using the `create clone of` block, the programmer tells Scratch to make an identical copy of a sprite at that moment. The copy, or clone, appears on the stage and can run its own scripts independently. In Scratch 3.0, clones inherit the original sprite’s costumes, sounds, and **scripts**, just as twins share the same DNA but can wear different clothes and stand in different places. Each clone can have its own local data, such as its x-y position, direction, and size, while sharing the same code. Programmers use clones when they want many similar actors on the stage — falling raindrops over Kerala during the monsoon, a swarm of fireflies in a Bengaluru park, or a fleet of buses on a busy Mumbai road — without copying and pasting the whole sprite.
Together, custom blocks and clones **simplify** large programs. The custom block turns repeated code into a reusable **command**, and the clone turns one sprite into many. They are both examples of abstraction in computing: the programmer hides a complicated pattern behind a simple idea. In an ICSE Class 7 project, a student might write a custom block called `hop` with a parameter `height`, and then use `create clone of myself` to produce a family of hopping rabbits that behave the same way but land at different spots on the stage. When a project is built with these blocks, the scripts become shorter, easier to read, and easier to debug.
eli5: In Scratch, you can make your own special block that does a whole trick when you click it. You can also give it a number, like "jump 5 steps," and it jumps that many steps. A clone is like making photocopies of a sprite, so you can have many of them moving around together, all using the same code, without drawing each one.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What is the difference between a custom block and a clone in Scratch? Name the block you use to create a clone and the area where you make a custom block.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A custom block is a new named **procedure** that a programmer builds to group repeated actions together. It is found under the "My Blocks" category by clicking the "Make a Block" button. It is a reusable **command** that can be called from many places in a script. A **clone**, on the other hand, is a runtime **duplicate** of an existing sprite, created by the `create clone of` block found in the "Control" category. While a custom block helps **simplify** code by hiding a sequence of steps under one name, a clone helps create many identical sprites that can act independently on the stage. For example, a student might make a custom block called `twinkle` that changes the sprite’s brightness and size, and then call it inside a `forever` loop. If the student then uses `create clone of myself`, one sprite becomes many twinkling stars on the stage, each running the same scripts but at its own position. The key difference is that the custom block is an abstraction of code, while the clone is a duplication of an object. The first lives in the "My Blocks" palette, and the second appears as a new sprite on the stage during the project.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Why is a custom block with a parameter better than copying the same script over and over again?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: Copying the same script over and over is like writing the same paragraph in ten different exercise books: it takes longer, wastes space, and a single spelling mistake means correcting all ten. A custom block with a **parameter** solves this by packing the repeated steps into one named **command** and letting the programmer change its behaviour with an input. Suppose a student wants to draw three circles with radii 30, 60, and 90 pixels. Without a custom block, the sprite list could end up holding three similar, long scripts, each with its own numbers. With a custom block named `drawCircle (radius)`, the student writes one definition, places the `radius` **parameter** inside every `move` and `turn` block that depends on it, and then calls `drawCircle (30)`, `drawCircle (60)`, and `drawCircle (90)`. If the radius values need to change, only the calls need to be edited; the definition stays the same. The script becomes shorter, easier to read, and much easier to debug. In the ICSE exam, such answers show the examiner that the student understands the purpose of abstraction and can use the vocabulary correctly: the custom block is a **procedure**, the input is a **parameter**, and the whole idea is to **simplify** the program.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A classmate says: "Clones are completely separate from the original sprite, so changing the original’s scripts after making the clones will not change the clones at all." Is this statement correct? Evaluate the claim with a balanced argument.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: This statement is mostly incorrect, though it contains a small grain of truth. In Scratch, a **clone** is a **duplicate** of a sprite that is created while the project runs by the `create clone of` block. It is true that each clone has its own local state: it can be at a different x-y position, face a different direction, wear a different costume, and hold different values in local variables. In that sense, a clone becomes an independent actor on the stage, and if the clone changes its own variable or position, the original does not follow it. However, the **scripts** and costumes that the clone uses come from the original sprite at the moment of creation, like twins sharing DNA from the same parents. The original is the master copy, and the clones inherit its code. If the original’s code is edited, the running behaviour of the project reflects the shared script. Therefore, saying that clones are "completely separate" is too strong. A better answer is that clones are partially independent: they are separate in position, look, and local data, but they depend on the original for their **scripts** and costumes. If a student wants different behaviour, the correct approach is not to pretend the clone is a different sprite with its own script panel, but to use the `when I start as a clone` hat, local variables, and custom-block **parameters** to make each clone behave differently while still sharing the same code. So the statement is misleading and would lose marks because it ignores the "twins sharing DNA" relationship.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A teacher asks you to make a Scratch animation of a bhel-puri vendor on the beach near Juhu in Mumbai. A crowd of seagulls should fly across the sky at different heights and speeds. Describe the scripts you would use, including one custom block and one clone command.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: First, I would draw or choose one seagull sprite. Inside the "My Blocks" category I would click "Make a Block" and name it `flyAcross (height) (speed)`, adding two **parameters**. The definition would start the seagull at the left side of the stage, set its y-position to the `height` **parameter**, and then repeat until it reaches the right edge, moving `speed` steps and switching to the next costume to flap its wings. This makes the custom block a reusable **procedure** for one seagull flight. Next, in the `when green flag clicked` script of the original seagull sprite, I would place a `repeat 8` loop and inside it put `create clone of myself`. To give each clone different data, the `when I start as a clone` hat can call `flyAcross (height) (speed)` with different values. For example, the first clone could be at y = 100 with speed 5, the second at y = 130 with speed 7, and so on. I could also use a `pick random` block so heights and speeds vary automatically. The original sprite can hide so only the clones are visible, or it can itself become one of the flying birds. This combination means the stage fills with flying seagulls from one master sprite, the scripts stay short, and the animation captures the busy Juhu beach atmosphere without having to draw eight separate seagulls.

diagnosticQuestions.question: Design a mini Scratch game in which the player controls a basket to catch falling mangoes from a tree. Explain how you would use a custom block and clones in your game.
diagnosticQuestions.answer: I would call the game "Alphonso Catcher" and set the stage to a mango orchard in Ratnagiri, Maharashtra. The player uses the left and right arrow keys to move a basket along the bottom of the stage. The falling fruit comes from a single mango sprite. I would make a custom block named `fall (delay)` with one **parameter** that tells the mango how long to wait before it starts dropping. Inside the definition, the mango goes to a random x-position at the top, `wait (delay) seconds`, then falls by changing y by negative amounts until it touches the bottom or the basket. If it touches the basket, the player gains a point; if it misses, the player loses a life. To create the stream of mangoes, the `when green flag clicked` script of the original mango sprite would hide itself and then run a `forever` loop with a `wait 2 seconds` and `create clone of myself`. Each new **clone** would start with the `when I start as a clone` hat and call `fall (delay)` with a different delay, perhaps increasing as the game gets harder. This way, there is only one mango sprite in the list, but many mangoes fall during the game. The custom block `fall` keeps the dropping logic in one place, and the clones let many mangoes fall at the same time, making the game challenging and fun while keeping the scripts easy to understand and modify.

masteryCriteria: The student must be able to create a custom block in Scratch under the "My Blocks" category, define it with at least one parameter, and correctly drag the parameter bubble into the blocks inside the definition so the block behaves differently for different inputs. The student must also be able to use the `create clone of [myself]` block together with the `when I start as a clone` hat to spawn multiple sprite copies that run the shared script at different positions, directions, or speeds. Finally, the student must be able to explain in their own words why a custom block with a parameter and a clone-based approach makes a program shorter, easier to read, and easier to debug than copying the same sprite or script repeatedly.

title: Scratch lists and string operations - data structures
subject: cs
definition:
A list in Scratch is a data structure that lets a program store and work with many related values inside one named container. Think of it as a vertical stack of labelled boxes, where each box holds one value and every box has a number, called its index, that tells you where it sits in the stack. When you create a list, you give it a name such as "Capitals" or "Classmates". You can then add items, delete items, insert items in the middle, replace an item, and read an item by using its index position. In Scratch, the first item you add becomes item 1, the next becomes item 2, and so on. This is different from some other computer languages, but for ICSE Class 7 you must remember that Scratch counting starts at 1.

Lists are useful because a single ordinary variable can hold only one value at a time. A list turns that one slot into a collection of slots. For example, a shopping list can hold "Milk", "Bread", "Butter" and "Tea" all together, and you can still ask the computer to show the second item or remove the last item. A to-do list, a name picker for a class competition, or the word list for a spelling game are all practical Scratch projects built around lists.

String operations are the blocks that let you manipulate text. A string is simply a sequence of characters such as a word, a sentence, or a name. The join block glues two pieces of text together, the length block counts how many characters are in a string, and the letter of block picks out one character by its position. If the string is "India", its length is 5, and letter 1 of "India" is "I". If you join "Jai" and "Hind" you get "JaiHind" unless you also add a space in between. Understanding these blocks is essential for word games, password checks, and any project that reads or builds messages.

Together, lists and string operations let you build programs that collect, search, and change information. A list gives you the container, the index gives you the address, and the string blocks give you the tools to shape the words inside.
eli5: A list is like a stack of numbered boxes that can each hold one thing. You can put new things in, take old things out, and look inside any box by saying its number. String blocks help you play with words: they can stick words together, count all the letters, or pick out just one letter. With lists and string blocks, you can make games, pick a random name, or build a smart to-do list.

misconceptions.belief: Many students think the first item of a list is item 0, just because they have read that some computer programs count from 0. CISCE examiners have observed that candidates become confused between the first index of an array and the first index of a string. In Scratch, the first item is always item 1, and the first character is also letter 1. Remind yourself that Scratch does not use 0 as a starting index.

Students often believe that the join block automatically puts a space between words. The join block simply glues the two strings together exactly as they are. "Jai" joined with "Hind" becomes "JaiHind". If you want "Jai Hind", you must join three things: "Jai", a space, and "Hind". Examiners have reported that vague string-handling code, especially when extracting characters and finding lengths, comes from not understanding that every character counts, including spaces.

Learners sometimes try to squeeze several values into one ordinary variable instead of making a list. For example, writing "Milk,Bread,Butter" into a single variable does not turn it into a list. A list is a separate data structure that is created in the Data category. You must use the list-specific add, delete, and item blocks to work with its contents.

diagnosticQuestions.question: What is the difference between a Scratch variable and a Scratch list, and how do you access a particular value in a list?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: A Scratch variable is designed to store one value at a time, such as the number 7 or the word "Delhi". A list, on the other hand, is a data structure that can hold many values together under one name. You can think of a variable as a single box and a list as a column of numbered boxes. To access a particular value in a list, you use the item block from the Data category. For example, if you have a list called "Fruits" and it contains "Mango", "Apple", "Banana", "Guava" in that order, then item 1 of Fruits is "Mango", item 2 is "Apple", and item 4 is "Guava". If the question asks for the last item, you can either remember the count or use the length of the list to find the highest index. The key idea is that the index tells the computer which box to open, and in Scratch the first box is number 1.

diagnosticQuestions.question: A student writes the following in Scratch: set [my list v] to [Mango,Apple,Banana]. Why does the script not create a list with three separate items, and what should the student do instead?
diagnosticQuestions.answer: The student has made the mistake of using a variable block to hold one piece of text. The set variable to block stores a single value, so "Mango,Apple,Banana" becomes one long string, not three list items. To create a list with three separate items, the student should first create a list called "my list" from the Data category, then use the add thing to my list block three times: first add "Mango", then add "Apple", then add "Banana". After that, item 1 of my list will be "Mango", item 2 will be "Apple", and item 3 will be "Banana". If the student wants to put all three values into the list at once, the only correct way in the standard Scratch interface is to add them one by one, because each add block adds one new item to the end of the list.
